speaker: provenzano
text: I'd like to welcome everybody to our council meeting. I wanna thank our broadcasting partners and our reporting partners for broadcasting our meetings and reporting on it. Before we get going, I just wanna make a couple of brief comments. We recognize that Ontario is setting records right now and the number of COVID cases we're seeing across the province. We've still been, I think, relatively fortunate in Algonquin-Sault Ste. Marie, but nonetheless, we've seen our cases increase here. It's very clear that the variants of concern are more transmissible and they're having a deleterious effect on a number of people who aren't fortunate enough to catch the virus. So I'd just like to just keep things simple and just ask the community to focus on a couple of simple rules. We've had a lot of rules thrown at us and there's been a lot that's changed over the last year, but I think I would boil it down simply this way. Stay home as much as you can. When you have to go out to engage in one of the activities that's permissible or you have to go to work, make sure that you wear a mask and you physically distance. So stay home as much as you can. When you have to go out, wear a mask and physically distance. Do not have social gatherings or encourage social gatherings or participate in anyone else's social gatherings. And if you have any symptoms, make sure that you get a test and you make sure that you self-isolate until you get that test back. So I think it's important that we all focus on following those simple rules. And I'm sure if we do, we will come out of this stronger. And in the meantime, this is obviously having a significant effect on a lot of entrepreneurs and local business people, especially our restaurant industry. I want to encourage people to support local as much as you can. There's a great social media initiative out there that Greg Lefebvre started, We Got Your Back, and it encourages people to support local restaurants and eateries directly. I would encourage everyone in the community to be mindful of the fact that we have a lot of business people in the community that are challenged or that are having a difficult time. And as and when you can, obviously following all proper public health guidelines, it'd be great to support them. When it is your turn to get a vaccine and you can't get a vaccine, we would certainly encourage that. We've had good uptake and response in our community. And I want to thank really all the stakeholders that are working on that project. I think they're delivering the vaccine efficiently when it gets to our community. I want to thank and recognize GoM Public Health and specifically the GoM Ontario Health Team for their work and all the community agencies supporting them in their work. And we'll keep on working together here. Keep yourself safe, keep your family safe. And by doing that, we'll help keep our community at large safe. Madam Clerk, if you could please start the meeting.

speaker: provenzano
text: So I want to recognize before I read this proclamation, recognize and thank the good folks at SOYA who have historically for a number of years done really great and important work in our community and they've been great to work with and I'm happy to do this proclamation at its request. Whereas overall, there was a 38.2% increase in opioid related deaths across Ontario in the first 15 weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is 695 deaths. And the opioid rate and emergency department visits in the province of Ontario were approximately 1.5 times higher in 2020 compared to 2018 and 2019. Whereas Algoma had the highest opioid related deaths in hospital admission rates in Ontario in 2020. And many people with substance use disorders face significant barriers in accessing treatment. Whereas the deaths of adults aged from 20 to 49 is increasing at an alarming rate. And the study by the government of Canada found that the rate of opioid related deaths in Ontario has tripled in the past 15 years and the most significant increase in young adults. Whereas city council passed a resolution on April 23rd, 2018 that recognized the opioid crisis along with the challenging and important work being undertaken by local healthcare providers, frontline workers, SOIA, HIV AIDS Resource Program, Ontario Aboriginal HIV AIDS Strategy and the Drug Strategy Committee and committed to continue to support that work. Whereas city council remains committed to supporting the efforts of our community, raising awareness about this issue and combating the stigma associated with opioid addiction. Therefore, I Christian Provenzano as Mayor of the City of Sault Ste. Marie do hereby proclaim April 16th, 2021 as the National Day of Action on the Overdose Epidemic here in the City of Sault Ste. Marie. Thank you.

speaker: waynegreco
text: Good evening, Mr. Mayor and Council. My name is Wayne Greco, Chair of the Sault Ste. Marie Public Library Board. Joining me in the presentation is Matthew McDonald, our CEO. On behalf of the Board of Directors, we'd like to thank you for the opportunity to talk about our 2020 Annual Report. In a time of uncertainty and a lot of COVID-related problems, we want to share with council our good news story. Despite doing continuing work on the city and the citizens of Sault Ste. Marie, the library has made efforts to reinvent itself and provide service to the community. We value the input of council as we move forward in the coming year. Please join us or try to join us in our 125th year of celebration this coming summer. Hopefully we'll be in person. Matthew's going to take you through some of the highlights of our 2020 Annual Report. Thank you again.

speaker: hughmacdonald
text: So I can take you through some highlights or I could just answer a few questions if you have them regarding the report.

speaker: provenzano
text: Oh, Matthew, you're welcome. I just didn't have a presentation attached to our agenda here, so I didn't know if you were making one, but if you were making one and sharing your screen, that's completely fine.

text: I just had some comments regarding the report itself.

speaker: provenzano
text: Okay, go ahead. We're in your hands.

speaker: hughmacdonald
text: Okay. So as you're aware, the year started out pretty well for the library. We actually received the Chamber of Commerce Award for Accessibility for the newly opened North Branch and our program was going strong. We had lots of visitors. The library was involved in a lot of activity in the community and then COVID happened and the library temporarily closed its doors. In our Annual Report, you'll see a timeline of all the significant events that happened for the library during the year. And though closed, not all the library services were disrupted. We continue to offer online services to our community and these included information databases, services such as our OverDrive and our Hoopla, which allows you to download eBooks and audio books, which was really important for our community members who were stuck at home and who are stuck at home to be able to access materials for education and entertainment. By May, when the government's restrictions lessened, we did transition to a new contactless service model. And in summer, along with Suburay's library, we were one of the first in Northern Ontario to open up and offer in-person services. So I think that's a big accomplishment on our part. We adapted. We provided a new Reader's Advisory Service, Surprise Reads for Kids, which established a way to help families who are unable to browse our shelves. So our staff are gathering materials based on the children's interests and making sure that we're getting books into their hands. Our programming also changed. They had to. So many people come to visit us, and then we had to transition so that we were visiting them in their living rooms. So our story times went online. We offer takeaway crafts for children through our curbside service during the summer and winter breaks. We gave online tutorials. We engaged the community electronically with programs such as our online Lego Club, a virtual author palooza, which highlighted many of our local authors. And we participated in cultural days online. We did what we could to keep our community engaged, learning, and entertained during one of the most difficult years this generation's ever seen. And throughout the annual report, you will find more information about these activities and the reach they had. Though closed to the public, our time was not idle. We did manage to complete several construction projects at the James L. MacIntyre Centennial Library during that time. And we updated much of our wayfinding to be bilingual thanks to a grant from the Ministry of Francophone Affairs. A very large project, which we did highlight at the budget deliberations, was the Sue Starr Archives, which we received at the end of last year. When the Sue Starr closed its offices, they had one month to vacate. And our staff acted quickly to relocate those collections to new archival space at the North Branch and to the local history collection at the James L. MacIntyre Centennial Library. And this collection is going to be an invaluable source for information for our community for years to come. The Sault Ste. Marie Public Library has been an institution that has existed for 125 years. And this is the second pandemic that the library has seen since it was established in 1896. Through all that time, the library has demonstrated that it is an invaluable resource to the community. And I believe our annual report demonstrates that. It has also proven that it is a resilient, adaptive organization that continues to evolve with our community and to meet our community's needs. And we've really proven that over this last year. So on behalf of the board and staff, I want to thank you for your continued support of the library and the community at Sears.

And whereas Sault Ste. Marie over the last 20 years has experienced increasing assessment values in some neighborhoods, but not others, at the same time as having an aggregate in year new growth rate of less than 1%. And whereas Sault Ste. Marie has access to detailed mapping from the innovation center that shows these geographic areas of assessment growth versus stagnation. And whereas it is in the interest of all Sault Ste. Marie rate payers to ensure that assessment distribution is as evenly spread through the city as possible and that new growth does not come at additional cost to the existing levy. And whereas new development is one of the main sources of new assessment growth, provided that new development does not shift assessment value away from another area of the city. And whereas Sault Ste. Marie is the largest city in Ontario without development charges or a cost recovery mechanism for planning charges, both of which are key tools for a municipality to ensure that growth does not create assessment decline and stagnation elsewhere. And whereas the city of Sault Ste. Marie is examining options for new growth community improvement plans, many of which in comparative municipalities provide development charges, exemptions for certain types of zones or needed development. Marie to adopt further tools to ensure that the cost of new development accurately reflects the cost to the general levy.
